title: A Simple Way To Have Better Classroom Management Next Year
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin recommends a quick exercise for improving next year's classroom management: listing the five most disruptive, annoying, or stressful misbehaviors from the previous year, then matching each to an existing classroom rule, creating a new rule if none applies. Beyond simply auditing a rule set, the real value comes from modeling those same misbehaviors, deliberately and with some exaggeration, in front of new students during the first week, since demonstrating what not to do makes the absurdity of the behavior obvious and memorable. He argues that because the modeling happens before students have had a chance to misbehave, it doesn't single anyone out personally even though many students may recognize themselves in it. The piece suggests extending the exercise across the last five years of misbehavior to ensure comprehensive rule coverage, while focusing modeling efforts on the top five most common offenses as representative examples. It closes by tying this proactive modeling, combined with consistent follow-through, to markedly better behavior than the previous year.
points: A quick end-of-year exercise: list the five most disruptive misbehaviors from the past year and match each to an existing classroom rule, adding new rules as needed.
The real power of the exercise comes from deliberately modeling those exact misbehaviors for new students during the first week of school.
Modeling misbehavior with some exaggeration highlights its absurdity in a way students understand and remember.
Because modeling happens before students have misbehaved, it doesn't single out any individual student personally, even if some recognize themselves.
Extending the audit across the last five years of experienced misbehavior helps ensure the rule set has comprehensive coverage.
quotes: The way it works is to list the five most disruptive, annoying , and stressful misbehaviors you witnessed last school year.
Now, draw a line from each misbehavior to the rule it breaks. If you can’t do this, then you need to create another rule.
You see, whatever misbehavior you model—as in how not to behave —you’re less likely to get from your students.

It communicates in a way students understand why such misbehavior is wrong and how it tramples on the rights of others. In fact, if modeled explicitly and followed by your promise to hold your students accountable, they’re loathe to repeat it.

And because it comes at the beginning of the year, before they can engage in such behavior, they won’t be offended. You’re not poking fun at anyone personally. However, many will see themselves in the behavior.
